what-every-door-direct-mail-actually-is.title: What Every Door Direct Mail Actually Is
what-every-door-direct-mail-actually-is.description: A plain-language explanation of USPS EDDM, how it differs from a purchased mailing list, and why it can reach a neighborhood for less.
what-every-door-direct-mail-actually-is.body:
If you've never advertised offline before, "EDDM" probably isn't a term you've run into. It stands for Every Door Direct Mail, and it's a program the United States Postal Service runs specifically so a business can mail every address on a carrier route without needing a single name, phone number, or purchased list. The mail carrier who already walks that route every day simply adds your piece to what they're delivering that day, to every stop along the way.

That last part is the whole idea, and it's worth sitting with for a second. A normal piece of addressed mail needs a name and address tied to it before the Postal Service will deliver it, which is why direct mail has historically meant buying a list first. EDDM skips that step entirely. You're not targeting people, you're targeting a route, and the route is public information the Postal Service will hand you for free.

## Why a route beats a list

A purchased mailing list is a snapshot. People move, sell their house, change their name, or simply never should have been on the list in the first place, and none of that gets caught until you're paying for postage on a piece that lands with someone who moved out two years ago. A carrier route doesn't have that problem, because it isn't a list of people, it's a list of addresses the mail already goes to. Whoever lives there right now gets your postcard, renter or owner, longtime resident or someone who moved in last week.

That also means EDDM naturally includes renters, who a lot of purchased homeowner lists quietly leave out. For plenty of local service categories, renters call just as often as homeowners do, and a list built around homeownership records misses a meaningful slice of the neighborhood before you've mailed a single piece.

The tradeoff is that you're not choosing individual households by income, age, or any other filter the way a purchased list might let you. You're choosing a geography instead. For a local business, that's usually the right tradeoff anyway: someone two streets from your shop is a better prospect than a stranger three towns over who happens to match a demographic filter, filter or no filter.

The other piece worth understanding is what you're actually paying for. USPS EDDM postage is priced per piece at a flat retail rate, and it's genuinely cheaper than addressed first-class mail because the Postal Service isn't sorting by name, just by route and by stop. Design and printing are separate costs on top of that if you're doing it entirely on your own, which is where a lot of the total cost of a mailer actually comes from.

That's the whole mechanism. No mailing list to buy or clean, no names to match to addresses, just a real route the carrier already walks, and every address on it getting your piece the same day. Once that clicks, the rest of the decisions, like which route to pick and what to put on the card, get a lot more concrete. If you want to see what a route actually looks like near your business before committing to anything, it's worth checking what one would reach.

your-carrier-route-is-a-better-list-than.title: Your Carrier Route Is a Better List Than You Could Buy
your-carrier-route-is-a-better-list-than.description: Why a real USPS carrier route stays more accurate over time than any purchased mailing list, and what that means for a local business.
your-carrier-route-is-a-better-list-than.body:
Every mailing list starts going stale the moment it's compiled. Someone moves, a name changes, a household that should never have been on a homeowner list in the first place gets included anyway because the data provider's records were a year out of date. You pay for the list once, but you pay for its mistakes every time you mail it, because postage doesn't know or care that the person you're reaching moved out eighteen months ago.

A USPS carrier route doesn't have that problem, for a simple reason: it was never a list of people to begin with. It's a list of stops a mail carrier walks or drives every single day, rain or shine, whether or not anyone on that street ever opted into anything. Every Door Direct Mail piggybacks on that existing route, so whoever actually lives at each address right now is who gets your postcard, not whoever lived there when a data company last updated its records.

## The list you didn't have to build

Think about what goes into a purchased mailing list: someone compiled property records, cross-referenced them against other data sources, tried to filter for homeowners or a certain income band, and sold you the result as a snapshot in time. Every one of those steps is a place for the list to be wrong, and none of those steps happen with a carrier route, because there's nothing to compile. The Postal Service already knows exactly which addresses are active on a route, because it delivers to every one of them every day regardless of who's advertising.

That also means a carrier route naturally covers people a purchased list often misses on purpose. Homeowner lists, by definition, skip renters, and depending on the neighborhood that can be a large share of the households nearby. If your business doesn't particularly care whether the person calling owns or rents, a homeowner-only list isn't targeting for you, it's just leaving money on the table before you've spent a dollar on postage.

None of this means a purchased list is never the right tool. If you genuinely need to reach people outside a defined geography, or you're filtering on something a carrier route truly can't tell you, a list still has its place. But for a local business whose customers are, almost by definition, people who live or work nearby, the geography is the target, not an afterthought to filter around. A carrier route delivers exactly that geography, completely, without you first paying someone to guess at it.

The practical upshot is that you're not really choosing between two versions of the same thing when you compare a mailing list to a carrier route. You're choosing between a snapshot that degrades from the day you buy it, and a route that's current because the Postal Service walks it today, tomorrow, and the day after. If you're weighing how to reach the neighborhood around your business, it's worth looking at what your actual route covers before pricing out a list instead.
